claims.text: Adding approximately 0.05–0.1 at.% boron during melting promotes boron segregation at grain boundaries.
Trace boron addition refines the eutectic lamellar microstructure.
Trace boron addition simultaneously increases yield strength and ductility relative to a boron-free alloy.
The starting alloy has an as-cast, multiphase lamellar microstructure.
Fine boride particles mediate refinement of the eutectic lamellar structure.
Boron addition lowers grain-boundary interfacial energy.
The boron-refined microstructure hinders dislocation motion.
The boron-refined microstructure delays crack propagation.
Hindering dislocation motion and delaying crack propagation enable concurrent improvements in strength and ductility.
The boron-doped alloy will have approximately 10–20% greater yield strength than the identically processed boron-free baseline.
The boron-doped alloy will maintain or slightly improve ductility relative to the boron-free baseline.
The proposed benefits depend on keeping boron content within approximately 0.05–0.1 at.%.
Boron contents above the proposed range may form coarse, brittle boride phases.
Highly oxidizing environments may reduce the expected benefits of boron addition.
Temperatures above approximately 900 °C may reduce the expected benefits of boron addition.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility changes may vary with processing conditions and small compositional differences.
The direction of the proposed strength and ductility improvements is supported by preliminary evidence.

contradictions.description: The experiment calls the two sample sets compositionally identical while also specifying that one set contains 0.05–0.1 at.% boron and the other contains no boron. They can only be identical in their non-boron constituents or nominal base composition.
